newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turks hopeful on economy after data, Telekom ruling.
newsitem.headline: Turks hopeful on economy after data, Telekom ruling.

text.p: The Turkish government's hopes of fulfilling ambitious economic plans were bolstered on Friday by better-than-expected budget figures and by market reaction to approval of key telecommunications privatisation.
Finance Minister Abdullatif Sener said the 1996 budget deficit was 1,215 trillion lira ($10.6 billion) compared with an earlier estimate of 1,300 trillion lira.
"An efficient economic management and strong tax collection enabled us to achieve better results than we expected in 1996," he told a news conference.

His comments came a day after the constitutional court ruled in favour of the state telecommunication company's sell-off, which analysts say could bring in about $3.5 billion to state coffers when the first tranche of up to 10 percent is sold off in the second half of this year.
The Istanbul stock market soared on the Telekom news. The IMKB National-100 .XU100 closed 11.17 percent higher on Friday and is up around 50 percent since the start of the year.
Sener said growth of the budget deficit was limited by improved tax collection, which analysts say is key to structural reforms.
"We achieved a 107.3 percent rise in tax collection although we were expecting 98 percent," Sener said.

"Privatisation revenues are a major part of the government's 1997 budget targets and it is understood that these will be realised after the legal obstacles are cleared by the constitutional court," he said.
He said budget revenues in 1996 amounted to 2,736 trillion lira against expenditures of 3,951 trillion lira.
"Our government is determined to attain a balanced budget through necessary revenue resources in 1997," he said.

The Islamist-led government, which targeted a zero budget deficit for 1997, has unveiled three sets of revenue raising packages including the privatisation of Turk Telekom, and hopes to raise $30 billion from the measures over an unspecified time to close fiscal and trade deficits.
"With this decision of the constitutional court the way is opened for the rest of privatisation," Deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller said after Thursday's Turk Telekom court ruling.
The court rejected all but a minor objection by 116 MPs, who said the law governing the privatisation of Turk Telekom was against the constitution.
The government also aims to privatise big petroleum and steel companies and expects $5 billion from sell-offs this year.
"A balanced budged is a sine qua non condition to fight high inflation, unfair income distribution and unemployment," Sener said. Annual wholesale inflation was 84.9 percent in 1996.

He said interest rates would continue to fall this year and this would take some of the cash burden off the shoulders of the Treasury, which is already under pressure from foreign debts of $78 billion and domestic debts of nearly 3,000 trillion lira ($26 billion).
The government has promised that in 1997 it will speed up privatisations, which have raised only $3 billion since the programme was launched in 1986, despite bold revenue pledges each year.
Several government ministers have said about $750 million is expected from privatisations in January alone.

The Privatisation Administration tendered for three state banks this week -- Etibank, Anadolubank and Denizbank -- and obtained bids at open auctions totalling $320.5 million. The High Board of Privatisation is yet to approve the bids.
($=115,000 Turkish lira)
